strings.b-00-meta.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.0: After this lesson you can explain how an electric current produces a magnetic field and how a compass needle shows it.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.1: After this lesson you can describe magnetic field lines and use the right-hand thumb rule for a straight current-carrying conductor.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.2: After this lesson you can explain the fields of a circular loop, a solenoid and an electromagnet.
strings.b-00-meta.objectives.3: After this lesson you can use Fleming's left-hand rule for the force on a current-carrying conductor and explain the safety parts of a domestic circuit.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.0.definition: The region around a magnet where its force can be detected.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.1.definition: A line that shows the path a hypothetical free north pole would tend to move along; it represents a magnetic field.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.2.definition: A rule for the direction of the field around a straight current-carrying wire: thumb along the current, curled fingers along the field lines.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.3.definition: A rule for the force on a current-carrying conductor: forefinger along the field, middle finger along the current, thumb along the force.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.4.definition: A cylindrical coil with many turns of wire; its field is like that of a bar magnet.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.5.definition: A soft iron core wrapped with a coil of insulated copper wire, which becomes magnetic when current flows.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.6.definition: The red-insulated domestic supply wire, called positive.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.7.definition: The black-insulated domestic supply wire, called negative.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.8.definition: The green-insulated safety wire connected to a metal plate deep in the earth.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.9.definition: A safety device that melts and breaks the circuit when current becomes too high.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.10.definition: A direct contact between live and neutral wires that makes current increase abruptly.
strings.b-00-meta.glossary.11.definition: Magnetic Resonance Imaging, a technique that uses the body's magnetic field to make images for diagnosis.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.0: Hold a small compass near a straight copper wire. Before current flows, the needle rests in one direction. When you pass current through the wire, the needle deflects. This simple observation is the door into this chapter.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.1: The deflection means that the electric current through the copper wire has produced a magnetic effect. Electricity and magnetism are linked. A current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.2: In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted accidentally found that a compass needle got deflected when an electric current passed through a metallic wire placed nearby. This showed that electricity and magnetism were related phenomena.
strings.b-01.paragraphs.3: Oersted's name is used for the unit of magnetic field strength, the oersted.
strings.b-02.question: A compass needle placed near a straight copper wire deflects when current is passed through the wire. What does this show?
strings.b-02.options.0: The wire has become a permanent magnet.
strings.b-02.options.1: The electric current has produced a magnetic effect.
strings.b-02.options.2: The compass needle has lost its magnetism.
strings.b-02.explanation: The deflection of the compass needle shows that the current through the copper wire has produced a magnetic effect.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.0: A compass needle is a small bar magnet. Its north-seeking end points approximately north and is called the north pole; its south-seeking end points approximately south and is called the south pole. Like poles repel, while unlike poles attract.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.1: Bring a magnet near iron filings and the filings arrange in a pattern. The magnet exerts a force in the region around it. That region is said to have a magnetic field.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.2: The lines along which the iron filings align are magnetic field lines. The direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction in which a north pole of a compass needle moves there.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.3: Field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole. Inside the magnet, they run from south pole to north pole, so field lines are closed curves.
strings.b-03.paragraphs.4: The closeness of field lines shows strength: crowded lines mean a stronger field. No two field lines cross, because at a crossing a compass needle would have to point in two directions at once, which is impossible.
strings.b-04.caption: Field lines around a bar magnet. They leave the north pole and enter the south pole.
strings.b-05.question: Why does a compass needle get deflected when brought near a bar magnet?
strings.b-05.options.0: The magnet's magnetic field exerts a force on the small magnet that is the compass needle.
strings.b-05.options.1: The compass needle becomes electrically charged.
strings.b-05.options.2: The bar magnet removes the needle's magnetism.
strings.b-05.options.3: The air between them pushes the needle.
strings.b-05.explanation: A compass needle is a small bar magnet, so a nearby magnet's field exerts a force on it and turns it.
strings.b-06.title: How to draw magnetic field lines around a bar magnet
strings.b-06.steps.0.title: Fix the paper and magnet
strings.b-06.steps.0.detail: Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board and place a bar magnet in the centre. Mark the boundary of the magnet.
strings.b-06.steps.1.title: Start near the north pole
strings.b-06.steps.1.detail: Place a small compass near the north pole of the magnet. The south pole of the needle points towards the north pole of the magnet, and the north pole of the compass is directed away from the magnet's north pole.
strings.b-06.steps.2.title: Mark and step forward
strings.b-06.steps.2.detail: Mark the position of the two ends of the needle. Move the compass to a new position so that its south pole occupies the position previously occupied by its north pole.
strings.b-06.steps.3.title: Continue to the south pole
strings.b-06.steps.3.detail: Proceed step by step until you reach the south pole of the magnet. Join the points marked on the paper by a smooth curve. This curve represents a field line.
strings.b-06.steps.4.title: Draw more lines
strings.b-06.steps.4.detail: Repeat the procedure and draw as many lines as you can. You get a pattern of magnetic field lines around the magnet.
strings.b-07.question: Which of the following is a property of magnetic field lines?
strings.b-07.options.0: They emerge from the south pole and merge at the north pole outside the magnet.
strings.b-07.options.1: They are closed curves and do not cross one another.
strings.b-07.options.3: They exist only inside the magnet.
strings.b-07.explanation: Field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole; inside the magnet they run from south to north, so they form closed curves. No two field lines cross.
strings.b-08.question: Why don't two magnetic field lines intersect each other?
strings.b-08.options.0: Because at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
strings.b-08.options.1: Because magnetic field lines are always straight.
strings.b-08.options.2: Because the field is zero everywhere.
strings.b-08.explanation: At a crossing, the field would have two directions at the same point, so a compass needle would have to point in two directions at once.
strings.b-09.question: Which two methods can produce a magnetic field?
strings.b-09.options.0: By a permanent magnet and by an electric current.
strings.b-09.options.1: By heating a wire and by cooling a magnet.
strings.b-09.options.2: By a fuse and by an earth wire.
strings.b-09.options.3: By a neutral wire and by a live wire.
strings.b-09.explanation: A magnet has a magnetic field around it, and a current-carrying conductor also produces a magnetic field.
strings.b-10.paragraphs.0: Pass current through a long straight copper wire. Sprinkle iron filings on a cardboard through which the wire passes. The filings form concentric circles around the wire. These circles are the magnetic field lines.
strings.b-10.paragraphs.1: If you reverse the current, the direction of the field lines reverses. If you increase the current, the compass deflection increases, so the field is stronger. If you move the compass farther from the wire, the deflection decreases, so the field is weaker.
strings.b-10.paragraphs.2: The field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles centred on the wire.
strings.b-11.question: Which of the following correctly describes the magnetic field near a long straight wire?
strings.b-11.options.0: The field consists of straight lines perpendicular to the wire.
strings.b-11.options.1: The field consists of straight lines parallel to the wire.
strings.b-11.options.2: The field consists of radial lines originating from the wire.
strings.b-11.options.3: The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
strings.b-11.explanation: Iron filings around a straight current-carrying wire arrange themselves in concentric circles centred on the wire.
strings.b-12.title: Using the right-hand thumb rule
strings.b-12.steps.0.title: Hold the conductor
strings.b-12.steps.0.detail: Imagine holding the current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand.
strings.b-12.steps.1.title: Point the thumb
strings.b-12.steps.1.detail: Point your thumb towards the direction of the current.
strings.b-12.steps.2.title: Curl the fingers
strings.b-12.steps.2.detail: Your fingers wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines of the magnetic field.
strings.b-12.steps.3.title: Remember the other name
strings.b-12.steps.3.detail: This rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule.
strings.b-13.problem: A current through a horizontal power line flows in east to west direction. What is the direction of magnetic field at a point directly below it and at a point directly above it?
strings.b-13.steps.0.title: Identify the current direction
strings.b-13.steps.0.detail: The current is in the east-west direction.
strings.b-13.steps.1.title: Apply the right-hand thumb rule
strings.b-13.steps.1.detail: Point the thumb of the right hand along the current; the fingers curl around the wire in the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-13.steps.2.title: View from the east end
strings.b-13.steps.2.detail: Viewed from the east end, the magnetic field at any point below or above the wire turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire.
strings.b-13.steps.3.title: View from the west end
strings.b-13.steps.3.detail: Viewed from the west end, the same field turns anti-clockwise.
strings.b-13.answer: The magnetic field at any point below or above the wire turns clockwise when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.
strings.b-14.caption: Concentric circular field lines around a straight wire whose current comes out of the page. The arrows show the field direction.
strings.b-15.question: If the current in a straight wire is reversed, what happens to the magnetic field lines around it?
strings.b-15.options.2: They become straight lines parallel to the wire.
strings.b-15.options.3: They become stronger but keep the same direction.
strings.b-15.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the magnetic field produced by the current.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.0: Bend the straight wire into a circular loop. At every point of the loop, the field lines are circles around the wire. As you move away from the wire, these circles become larger. At the centre of the loop, the arcs of these large circles appear as straight lines. Every section of the wire adds its field in the same direction inside the loop.
strings.b-16.paragraphs.1: If the coil has n turns, the field is n times as large as that of a single turn, because each turn carries current in the same direction and the fields add up.
strings.b-17.question: A circular loop of wire lies in the plane of a table. The current in the loop is clockwise when viewed from above. Using the right-hand rule, what is the direction of the magnetic field inside the loop?
strings.b-17.explanation: Curl the fingers of the right hand in the clockwise direction of the current; the thumb points into the table. Outside the loop the field lines return in the opposite direction.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.0: A solenoid is a coil with many circular turns wound in the shape of a cylinder. Its field lines are similar to those of a bar magnet. Inside the solenoid the field lines are straight and the field is uniform. One end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
strings.b-18.paragraphs.1: An electromagnet is made of a soft iron core wrapped with a coil of insulated copper wire. A current-carrying solenoid can magnetise a steel rod placed inside it.
strings.b-19.question: The magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid-carrying current
strings.b-19.options.1: decreases as we move towards its end.
strings.b-19.options.2: increases as we move towards its end.
strings.b-19.options.3: is the same at all points.
strings.b-19.explanation: Inside a long current-carrying solenoid the field lines are straight and the field is uniform, so it is the same at all points inside.
strings.b-20.question: The magnetic field in a given region is uniform. How is it represented by field lines?
strings.b-20.options.0: By parallel straight lines equally spaced.
strings.b-20.options.2: By radial lines from one point.
strings.b-20.options.3: By lines that cross one another.
strings.b-20.explanation: A uniform field has the same strength and direction everywhere, so its field lines are parallel and equally spaced straight lines.
strings.b-21.paragraphs.0: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. Suspend a small aluminium rod horizontally between the poles of a strong horse-shoe magnet and pass current through it. The rod is displaced. Reverse the current and the displacement reverses. Reverse the magnetic field and the force reverses again.
strings.b-21.paragraphs.1: The force is largest when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field. Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include electric motors, electric generators, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments.
strings.b-22.title: Using Fleming's left-hand rule
strings.b-22.steps.0.title: Stretch the fingers
strings.b-22.steps.0.detail: Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular.
strings.b-22.steps.1.title: Point the first finger
strings.b-22.steps.1.detail: Point the first finger in the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-22.steps.2.title: Point the second finger
strings.b-22.steps.2.detail: Point the second finger in the direction of the current.
strings.b-22.steps.3.title: Read the thumb
strings.b-22.steps.3.detail: The thumb then points in the direction of motion or the force acting on the conductor.
strings.b-23.problem: In Activity 12.7, a small aluminium rod AB is suspended horizontally from a stand. A strong horse-shoe magnet is placed so that its north pole is vertically below and its south pole is vertically above the rod. A current is passed through the rod from end B to end A, and the rod is displaced towards the left. Explain why the rod is displaced, and state what is observed if the direction of the current through the rod is reversed.
strings.b-23.steps.0.title: Note the direction of the magnetic field
strings.b-23.steps.0.detail: The north pole of the magnet is vertically below the rod and the south pole is vertically above it, so the magnetic field between the poles is directed upwards.
strings.b-23.steps.1.title: Note the direction of the current
strings.b-23.steps.1.detail: The current is passed through the rod from end B to end A.
strings.b-23.steps.2.title: Apply the force rule
strings.b-23.steps.2.detail: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. The force is perpendicular to both the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field, so we use Fleming's left-hand rule to find its direction.
strings.b-23.steps.3.title: Read the direction with Fleming's left-hand rule
strings.b-23.steps.3.detail: Point the first finger along the magnetic field (upwards) and the second finger along the current (from B to A). The thumb then gives the direction of the force on the rod, which is why the rod is displaced towards the left.
strings.b-23.steps.4.title: Reverse the current
strings.b-23.steps.4.detail: The direction of the force is reversed when the direction of current through the conductor is reversed. So the displacement is now towards the right. (The force is largest when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field, as it is here.)
strings.b-23.answer: The rod is displaced towards the left because the current-carrying rod experiences a force in the magnetic field, with direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the force, so the rod is then displaced towards the right.
strings.b-24.question: In Activity 12.7, a small aluminium rod AB is suspended between the poles of a strong horse-shoe magnet and a current is passed through it. The rod gets displaced. What does this show?
strings.b-24.options.0: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force.
strings.b-24.options.1: The aluminium rod has become a permanent magnet.
strings.b-24.options.2: The horse-shoe magnet has lost its magnetism.
strings.b-24.options.3: The current in the rod has stopped.
strings.b-24.explanation: The displacement of the rod suggests that a force is exerted on the current-carrying aluminium rod when it is placed in a magnetic field.
strings.b-25.question: In Activity 12.7, the direction of current through the rod AB is reversed. What is observed?
strings.b-25.options.0: The rod is now displaced in the opposite direction.
strings.b-25.options.1: The rod is displaced in the same direction as before.
strings.b-25.options.2: The rod is not displaced at all.
strings.b-25.options.3: The rod becomes a magnet and stays still.
strings.b-25.explanation: The direction of the force is reversed when the direction of current through the conductor is reversed. Changing the direction of the magnetic field by interchanging the poles also reverses the force.
strings.b-26.question: A positively-charged particle (alpha-particle) projected towards west is deflected towards north by a magnetic field. What is the direction of the magnetic field?
strings.b-26.explanation: Use Fleming's left-hand rule. The current is towards west and the force is towards north; the magnetic field must be upward.
strings.b-27.question: When is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
strings.b-27.options.0: When the current is parallel to the magnetic field.
strings.b-27.options.1: When the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
strings.b-27.options.3: When the conductor is outside the field.
strings.b-27.explanation: The displacement of the rod is largest when the direction of current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field.
strings.b-28.question: An electron beam moves horizontally from the back wall towards the front wall of a chamber. It is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of the magnetic field?
strings.b-28.explanation: The electron current is opposite to the electron motion. Using Fleming's left-hand rule with the force to the right gives a downward magnetic field.
strings.b-29.question: Which rule gives the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor, and which rule gives the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field?
strings.b-29.options.0: Fleming's left-hand rule; right-hand thumb rule
strings.b-29.options.1: Right-hand thumb rule; Fleming's left-hand rule
strings.b-29.options.2: Right-hand thumb rule; right-hand thumb rule
strings.b-29.options.3: Fleming's left-hand rule; Fleming's left-hand rule
strings.b-29.explanation: The right-hand thumb rule gives the field around a straight conductor, and Fleming's left-hand rule gives the force on a current-carrying conductor. The chapter does not state a rule for current induced by rotation; it only names electric generator as a device.
strings.b-30.paragraphs.0: In homes, electric power comes through mains, either by overhead poles or underground cables. The live wire usually has red insulation and is positive. The neutral wire has black insulation and is negative. In our country the potential difference between them is 220 V. The supply is AC at 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.
strings.b-30.paragraphs.1: At the meter-board, the wires pass through an electricity meter and a main fuse. Through the main switch they connect to line wires. Often two circuits are used: a 15 A circuit for high-power appliances such as geysers and air coolers, and a 5 A circuit for bulbs and fans.
strings.b-30.paragraphs.2: The earth wire has green insulation and is connected to a metal plate deep in the earth. It is a safety measure for appliances with metallic bodies. It provides a low-resistance path so that any leakage of current to the metallic body does not give the user a severe shock.
strings.b-30.paragraphs.3: Appliances are connected in parallel across live and neutral so that each gets the same potential difference. Each appliance has its own switch. A fuse prevents damage due to overloading. The Joule heating in the fuse melts it and breaks the circuit.
strings.b-30.paragraphs.4: Short-circuiting occurs when the live and neutral wires touch directly; the current increases abruptly. Overloading can also occur from an accidental hike in supply voltage or by connecting too many appliances to one socket.
strings.b-31.question: Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
strings.b-31.explanation: A fuse protects against overloading by melting, and the earth wire provides a safety path for leakage current.
strings.b-32.question: How does an electric fuse protect a domestic circuit?
strings.b-32.options.0: The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it and breaks the electric circuit.
strings.b-32.options.1: The fuse stores the extra current and supplies it later.
strings.b-32.options.2: The fuse raises the supply voltage.
strings.b-32.options.3: The fuse connects the live wire to the earth wire.
strings.b-32.explanation: A fuse prevents damage to the appliances and the circuit due to overloading by stopping the flow of unduly high electric current; the Joule heating in the fuse melts it to break the circuit.
strings.b-33.question: What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
strings.b-33.options.0: Connect too many appliances to a single socket.
strings.b-33.options.1: Avoid connecting too many appliances to a single socket and use a fuse of proper rating.
strings.b-33.options.2: Replace the earth wire with a live wire.
strings.b-33.options.3: Use only 15 A circuits for bulbs.
strings.b-33.explanation: Overloading can be caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket; a fuse protects the circuit if current becomes too high.
strings.b-34.question: At the time of short circuit, the current in the circuit
strings.b-34.explanation: When live and neutral wires touch directly, the current in the circuit abruptly increases.
strings.b-35.question: When does an electric short circuit occur?
strings.b-35.options.0: When the live wire and neutral wire come into direct contact.
strings.b-35.options.2: When the earth wire is connected to a metal plate.
strings.b-35.options.3: When the main switch is off.
strings.b-35.explanation: Direct contact between live and neutral wires is short-circuiting; this can happen when insulation is damaged or an appliance has a fault.
strings.b-36.question: What is the function of an earth wire, and why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
strings.b-36.options.0: It carries the normal current and increases the supply voltage.
strings.b-36.options.1: It provides a low-resistance path for leakage current so the user may not get a severe shock.
strings.b-36.options.2: It melts when current is too high.
strings.b-36.explanation: The metallic body is connected to the earth wire. If current leaks to the body, the earth wire keeps its potential at that of the earth and protects the user.
strings.b-37.question: Which statement is true?
strings.b-37.options.0: The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines.
strings.b-37.options.1: A wire with green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
strings.b-37.explanation: At the centre of a current-carrying circular coil the field lines appear as parallel straight lines. The green-insulated wire is the earth wire, not the live wire.
strings.b-38.paragraphs.0: Electric currents in the body, even weak ion currents along nerve cells, produce magnetic fields. These fields are very weak, about one-billionth of the earth's magnetic field. The heart and the brain are two main organs where the magnetic field produced is significant.
strings.b-38.paragraphs.1: The magnetic field inside the body is used in Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to obtain images of different body parts. Analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.
strings.b-39.question: Which technique uses the magnetic field inside the body to obtain images of different body parts for medical diagnosis?
strings.b-39.explanation: MRI uses the magnetic field inside the body to obtain images; analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.

lesson.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
objectives: After this lesson you can explain how an electric current produces a magnetic field and how a compass needle shows it.
After this lesson you can describe magnetic field lines and use the right-hand thumb rule for a straight current-carrying conductor.
After this lesson you can explain the fields of a circular loop, a solenoid and an electromagnet.
After this lesson you can use Fleming's left-hand rule for the force on a current-carrying conductor and explain the safety parts of a domestic circuit.

sections.title: A current can act like a magnet
paragraphs: Hold a small compass near a straight copper wire. Before current flows, the needle rests in one direction. When you pass current through the wire, the needle deflects. This simple observation is the door into this chapter.
The deflection means that the electric current through the copper wire has produced a magnetic effect. Electricity and magnetism are linked. A current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet.

In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted accidentally found that a compass needle got deflected when an electric current passed through a metallic wire placed nearby. This showed that electricity and magnetism were related phenomena.
Oersted's name is used for the unit of magnetic field strength, the oersted. In this chapter you will study magnetic fields and electromagnets, which use the magnetic effect of current.

sections.title: Magnetic field and field lines
paragraphs: A compass needle is a small bar magnet. Its north-seeking end points approximately north and is called the north pole; its south-seeking end points approximately south and is called the south pole. Like poles repel, while unlike poles attract.
Bring a magnet near iron filings and the filings arrange in a pattern. The magnet exerts a force in the region around it. That region is said to have a magnetic field.

The lines along which the iron filings align are magnetic field lines. You can draw them with a compass: place the compass near the north pole, mark the needle direction, move the compass so its south pole takes the old north-pole position, and continue step by step to the south pole; join the points smoothly.

The direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction in which a north pole of a compass needle moves there. Field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole. Inside the magnet, they run from south pole to north pole, so field lines are closed curves.

The closeness of field lines shows strength: crowded lines mean a stronger field. No two field lines cross, because at a crossing a compass needle would have to point in two directions at once, which is impossible.
A magnetic field can be produced by a permanent magnet or by an electric current.

sections.title: Magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire
paragraphs: Pass current through a long straight copper wire. Sprinkle iron filings on a cardboard through which the wire passes. The filings form concentric circles around the wire. These circles are the magnetic field lines.

If you reverse the current, the direction of the field lines reverses. If you increase the current, the compass deflection increases, so the field is stronger. If you move the compass farther from the wire, the deflection decreases, so the field is weaker.

To find the direction, use the right-hand thumb rule. Hold the current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand so that your thumb points along the current. Your fingers wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines. This is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule.

For a horizontal power line carrying current from east to west, the field at a point directly below or above the line turns clockwise when viewed from the east end and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.

sections.title: Circular loop, solenoid and electromagnet
paragraphs: Bend the straight wire into a circular loop. At every point of the loop, the field lines are circles around the wire. As you move away from the wire, these circles become larger. At the centre of the loop, the arcs of these large circles appear as straight lines. Every section of the wire adds its field in the same direction inside the loop.
If the coil has n turns, the field is n times as large as that of a single turn, because each turn carries current in the same direction and the fields add up.

A solenoid is a coil with many circular turns wound in the shape of a cylinder. Its field lines are similar to those of a bar magnet. Inside the solenoid the field lines are straight and the field is uniform. One end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
An electromagnet is made of a soft iron core wrapped with a coil of insulated copper wire. A current-carrying solenoid can magnetise a steel rod placed inside it.

sections.title: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
paragraphs: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. Suspend a small aluminium rod horizontally between the poles of a strong horse-shoe magnet and pass current through it. The rod is displaced. Reverse the current and the displacement reverses. Reverse the magnetic field and the force reverses again.

The force is largest when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field. In that case, use Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand mutually perpendicular. Point the first finger along the magnetic field and the second finger along the current; the thumb points along the force or motion of the conductor.

An electron entering a magnetic field at right angles also experiences a force. The current direction is taken opposite to the electron's motion. In the given case, the force is directed into the page.
Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include electric motors, electric generators, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments.

sections.title: Domestic electric circuits and safety
paragraphs: In homes, electric power comes through mains, either by overhead poles or underground cables. The live wire usually has red insulation and is positive. The neutral wire has black insulation and is negative. In our country the potential difference between them is 220 V. The supply is AC at 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.

At the meter-board, the wires pass through an electricity meter and a main fuse. Through the main switch they connect to line wires. Often two circuits are used: a 15 A circuit for high-power appliances such as geysers and air coolers, and a 5 A circuit for bulbs and fans.

The earth wire has green insulation and is connected to a metal plate deep in the earth. It is a safety measure for appliances with metallic bodies. It provides a low-resistance path so that any leakage of current to the metallic body does not give the user a severe shock.

Appliances are connected in parallel across live and neutral so that each gets the same potential difference. Each appliance has its own switch. A fuse prevents damage due to overloading. The Joule heating in the fuse melts it and breaks the circuit.

Short-circuiting occurs when the live and neutral wires touch directly; the current increases abruptly. Overloading can also occur from an accidental hike in supply voltage or by connecting too many appliances to one socket.

sections.title: Magnetism in medicine
paragraphs: Electric currents in the body, even weak ion currents along nerve cells, produce magnetic fields. These fields are very weak, about one-billionth of the earth's magnetic field. The heart and the brain are two main organs where the magnetic field produced is significant.
The magnetic field inside the body is used in Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to obtain images of different body parts. Analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.

glossary.definition: The region around a magnet where its force can be detected.
A line that shows the path a hypothetical free north pole would tend to move along; it represents a magnetic field.
A rule for the direction of the field around a straight current-carrying wire: thumb along the current, curled fingers along the field lines.
A rule for the force on a current-carrying conductor: forefinger along the field, middle finger along the current, thumb along the force.
A cylindrical coil with many turns of wire; its field is like that of a bar magnet.
A soft iron core wrapped with a coil of insulated copper wire, which becomes magnetic when current flows.
The red-insulated domestic supply wire, called positive.
The black-insulated domestic supply wire, called negative.
The green-insulated safety wire connected to a metal plate deep in the earth.
A safety device that melts and breaks the circuit when current becomes too high.
A direct contact between live and neutral wires that makes current increase abruptly.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging, a technique that uses the body's magnetic field to make images for diagnosis.

paragraphs: Hold a small compass near a straight copper wire. Before current flows, the needle rests in one direction. When you pass current through the wire, the needle deflects. This simple observation is the door into this chapter.
The deflection means that the electric current through the copper wire has produced a magnetic effect. Electricity and magnetism are linked. A current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet.

In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted accidentally found that a compass needle got deflected when an electric current passed through a metallic wire placed nearby. This showed that electricity and magnetism were related phenomena.
Oersted's name is used for the unit of magnetic field strength, the oersted.

spec.question: A compass needle placed near a straight copper wire deflects when current is passed through the wire. What does this show?
options: The wire has become a permanent magnet.
The electric current has produced a magnetic effect.
The compass needle has lost its magnetism.
The current has stopped.
spec.answer: The electric current has produced a magnetic effect.
spec.explanation: The deflection of the compass needle shows that the current through the copper wire has produced a magnetic effect.
spec.expected_understanding: Link a current-carrying wire with a magnetic effect.

paragraphs: A compass needle is a small bar magnet. Its north-seeking end points approximately north and is called the north pole; its south-seeking end points approximately south and is called the south pole. Like poles repel, while unlike poles attract.
Bring a magnet near iron filings and the filings arrange in a pattern. The magnet exerts a force in the region around it. That region is said to have a magnetic field.
The lines along which the iron filings align are magnetic field lines. The direction of the magnetic field at a point is the direction in which a north pole of a compass needle moves there.
Field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole. Inside the magnet, they run from south pole to north pole, so field lines are closed curves.

The closeness of field lines shows strength: crowded lines mean a stronger field. No two field lines cross, because at a crossing a compass needle would have to point in two directions at once, which is impossible.

spec.caption: Field lines around a bar magnet. They leave the north pole and enter the south pole.

spec.question: Why does a compass needle get deflected when brought near a bar magnet?
options: The magnet's magnetic field exerts a force on the small magnet that is the compass needle.
The compass needle becomes electrically charged.
The bar magnet removes the needle's magnetism.
The air between them pushes the needle.
spec.answer: The magnet's magnetic field exerts a force on the small magnet that is the compass needle.
spec.explanation: A compass needle is a small bar magnet, so a nearby magnet's field exerts a force on it and turns it.
spec.expected_understanding: Explain compass deflection using the magnetic field of a magnet.

spec.title: How to draw magnetic field lines around a bar magnet

steps.title: Fix the paper and magnet
steps.detail: Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board and place a bar magnet in the centre. Mark the boundary of the magnet.

steps.title: Start near the north pole
steps.detail: Place a small compass near the north pole of the magnet. The south pole of the needle points towards the north pole of the magnet, and the north pole of the compass is directed away from the magnet's north pole.

steps.title: Mark and step forward
steps.detail: Mark the position of the two ends of the needle. Move the compass to a new position so that its south pole occupies the position previously occupied by its north pole.

steps.title: Continue to the south pole
steps.detail: Proceed step by step until you reach the south pole of the magnet. Join the points marked on the paper by a smooth curve. This curve represents a field line.

steps.title: Draw more lines
steps.detail: Repeat the procedure and draw as many lines as you can. You get a pattern of magnetic field lines around the magnet.

spec.question: Which of the following is a property of magnetic field lines?
options: They emerge from the south pole and merge at the north pole outside the magnet.
They are closed curves and do not cross one another.
They cross at the poles.
They exist only inside the magnet.
spec.answer: They are closed curves and do not cross one another.
spec.explanation: Field lines emerge from the north pole and merge at the south pole; inside the magnet they run from south to north, so they form closed curves. No two field lines cross.
spec.expected_understanding: List the properties of magnetic field lines.

spec.question: Why don't two magnetic field lines intersect each other?
options: Because at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
Because magnetic field lines are always straight.
Because the field is zero everywhere.
Because iron filings cannot cross.
spec.answer: Because at the point of intersection the compass needle would point towards two directions, which is not possible.
spec.explanation: At a crossing, the field would have two directions at the same point, so a compass needle would have to point in two directions at once.
spec.expected_understanding: Give the reason field lines cannot cross.

spec.question: Which two methods can produce a magnetic field?
options: By a permanent magnet and by an electric current.
By heating a wire and by cooling a magnet.
By a fuse and by an earth wire.
By a neutral wire and by a live wire.
spec.answer: By a permanent magnet and by an electric current.
spec.explanation: A magnet has a magnetic field around it, and a current-carrying conductor also produces a magnetic field.
spec.expected_understanding: Name two ways of producing magnetic fields.

paragraphs: Pass current through a long straight copper wire. Sprinkle iron filings on a cardboard through which the wire passes. The filings form concentric circles around the wire. These circles are the magnetic field lines.

If you reverse the current, the direction of the field lines reverses. If you increase the current, the compass deflection increases, so the field is stronger. If you move the compass farther from the wire, the deflection decreases, so the field is weaker.
The field lines around a straight current-carrying wire are concentric circles centred on the wire.

spec.question: Which of the following correctly describes the magnetic field near a long straight wire?
options: The field consists of straight lines perpendicular to the wire.
The field consists of straight lines parallel to the wire.
The field consists of radial lines originating from the wire.
The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
spec.answer: The field consists of concentric circles centred on the wire.
spec.explanation: Iron filings around a straight current-carrying wire arrange themselves in concentric circles centred on the wire.
spec.expected_understanding: Recognise the shape of the field around a straight current-carrying wire.

steps.title: Hold the conductor
steps.detail: Imagine holding the current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand.

steps.title: Point the thumb
steps.detail: Point your thumb towards the direction of the current.

steps.title: Curl the fingers
steps.detail: Your fingers wrap around the conductor in the direction of the field lines of the magnetic field.

steps.title: Remember the other name
steps.detail: This rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule.

spec.problem: A current through a horizontal power line flows in east to west direction. What is the direction of magnetic field at a point directly below it and at a point directly above it?

steps.title: Identify the current direction
steps.detail: The current is in the east-west direction.

steps.title: Apply the right-hand thumb rule
steps.detail: Point the thumb of the right hand along the current; the fingers curl around the wire in the direction of the magnetic field.

steps.title: View from the east end
steps.detail: Viewed from the east end, the magnetic field at any point below or above the wire turns clockwise in a plane perpendicular to the wire.

steps.title: View from the west end
steps.detail: Viewed from the west end, the same field turns anti-clockwise.

spec.answer: The magnetic field at any point below or above the wire turns clockwise when viewed from the east end, and anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.

spec.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 360 360' role='img' aria-label='Cross-section of a straight wire with current out of the page and concentric circular magnetic field lines'><circle cx='180' cy='180' r='6' fill='#1C1B18'/><text x='180' y='210' font-family='Bricolage Grotesque, Arial, sans-serif' font-size='16' font-weight='700' fill='#1C1B18' text-anchor='middle'>wire</text><circle cx='180' cy='180' r='40' fill='none' stroke='#1C1B18' stroke-width='2.5'/><circle cx='180' cy='180' r='80' fill='none' stroke='#1C1B18' stroke-width='2.5'/><circle cx='180' cy='180' r='120' fill='none' stroke='#1C1B18' stroke-width='2.5'/><circle cx='180' cy='180' r='160' fill='none' stroke='#1C1B18' stroke-width='2.5'/><polygon points='172,140 182,135 182,145' fill='#1F3A9E'/><polygon points='172,100 182,95 182,105' fill='#1F3A9E'/><polygon points='172,60 182,55 182,65' fill='#1F3A9E'/><polygon points='172,20 182,15 182,25' fill='#1F3A9E'/><text x='180' y='330' font-family='Caveat, Segoe Print, Bradley Hand, cursive' font-size='22' font-weight='700' fill='#1F3A9E' text-anchor='middle'>current out of page</text></svg>
spec.caption: Concentric circular field lines around a straight wire whose current comes out of the page. The arrows show the field direction.

spec.question: If the current in a straight wire is reversed, what happens to the magnetic field lines around it?
options: Their direction reverses.
They disappear.
They become straight lines parallel to the wire.
They become stronger but keep the same direction.
spec.answer: Their direction reverses.
spec.explanation: Reversing the current reverses the direction of the magnetic field produced by the current.
spec.expected_understanding: Connect current direction with field direction.

paragraphs: Bend the straight wire into a circular loop. At every point of the loop, the field lines are circles around the wire. As you move away from the wire, these circles become larger. At the centre of the loop, the arcs of these large circles appear as straight lines. Every section of the wire adds its field in the same direction inside the loop.
If the coil has n turns, the field is n times as large as that of a single turn, because each turn carries current in the same direction and the fields add up.

spec.question: A circular loop of wire lies in the plane of a table. The current in the loop is clockwise when viewed from above. Using the right-hand rule, what is the direction of the magnetic field inside the loop?
options: Into the table.
Out of the table.
Along the table towards north.
The field inside is zero.
spec.answer: Into the table.
spec.explanation: Curl the fingers of the right hand in the clockwise direction of the current; the thumb points into the table. Outside the loop the field lines return in the opposite direction.
spec.expected_understanding: Use the right-hand rule for a circular loop.

paragraphs: A solenoid is a coil with many circular turns wound in the shape of a cylinder. Its field lines are similar to those of a bar magnet. Inside the solenoid the field lines are straight and the field is uniform. One end acts as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
An electromagnet is made of a soft iron core wrapped with a coil of insulated copper wire. A current-carrying solenoid can magnetise a steel rod placed inside it.

spec.question: The magnetic field inside a long straight solenoid-carrying current
options: is zero.
decreases as we move towards its end.
increases as we move towards its end.
is the same at all points.
spec.answer: is the same at all points.
spec.explanation: Inside a long current-carrying solenoid the field lines are straight and the field is uniform, so it is the same at all points inside.
spec.expected_understanding: Know that the field inside a long solenoid is uniform.

spec.question: The magnetic field in a given region is uniform. How is it represented by field lines?
options: By parallel straight lines equally spaced.
By concentric circles.
By radial lines from one point.
By lines that cross one another.
spec.answer: By parallel straight lines equally spaced.
spec.explanation: A uniform field has the same strength and direction everywhere, so its field lines are parallel and equally spaced straight lines.
spec.expected_understanding: Represent a uniform magnetic field by field lines.

paragraphs: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. Suspend a small aluminium rod horizontally between the poles of a strong horse-shoe magnet and pass current through it. The rod is displaced. Reverse the current and the displacement reverses. Reverse the magnetic field and the force reverses again.

The force is largest when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field. Devices that use current-carrying conductors and magnetic fields include electric motors, electric generators, loudspeakers, microphones and measuring instruments.

steps.title: Stretch the fingers
steps.detail: Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of your left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular.

steps.title: Point the first finger
steps.detail: Point the first finger in the direction of the magnetic field.

steps.title: Point the second finger
steps.detail: Point the second finger in the direction of the current.

steps.title: Read the thumb
steps.detail: The thumb then points in the direction of motion or the force acting on the conductor.

spec.problem: In Activity 12.7, a small aluminium rod AB is suspended horizontally from a stand. A strong horse-shoe magnet is placed so that its north pole is vertically below and its south pole is vertically above the rod. A current is passed through the rod from end B to end A, and the rod is displaced towards the left. Explain why the rod is displaced, and state what is observed if the direction of the current through the rod is reversed.

steps.title: Note the direction of the magnetic field
steps.detail: The north pole of the magnet is vertically below the rod and the south pole is vertically above it, so the magnetic field between the poles is directed upwards.

steps.title: Note the direction of the current
steps.detail: The current is passed through the rod from end B to end A.

steps.title: Apply the force rule
steps.detail: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. The force is perpendicular to both the direction of the current and the direction of the magnetic field, so we use Fleming's left-hand rule to find its direction.

steps.title: Read the direction with Fleming's left-hand rule
steps.detail: Point the first finger along the magnetic field (upwards) and the second finger along the current (from B to A). The thumb then gives the direction of the force on the rod, which is why the rod is displaced towards the left.

steps.title: Reverse the current
steps.detail: The direction of the force is reversed when the direction of current through the conductor is reversed. So the displacement is now towards the right. (The force is largest when the current is at right angles to the magnetic field, as it is here.)

spec.answer: The rod is displaced towards the left because the current-carrying rod experiences a force in the magnetic field, with direction given by Fleming's left-hand rule. Reversing the current reverses the direction of the force, so the rod is then displaced towards the right.

spec.question: In Activity 12.7, a small aluminium rod AB is suspended between the poles of a strong horse-shoe magnet and a current is passed through it. The rod gets displaced. What does this show?
options: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force.
The aluminium rod has become a permanent magnet.
The horse-shoe magnet has lost its magnetism.
The current in the rod has stopped.
spec.answer: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force.
spec.explanation: The displacement of the rod suggests that a force is exerted on the current-carrying aluminium rod when it is placed in a magnetic field.
spec.expected_understanding: State what the displacement of the rod in Activity 12.7 shows.

spec.question: In Activity 12.7, the direction of current through the rod AB is reversed. What is observed?
options: The rod is now displaced in the opposite direction.
The rod is displaced in the same direction as before.
The rod is not displaced at all.
The rod becomes a magnet and stays still.
spec.answer: The rod is now displaced in the opposite direction.
spec.explanation: The direction of the force is reversed when the direction of current through the conductor is reversed. Changing the direction of the magnetic field by interchanging the poles also reverses the force.
spec.expected_understanding: Relate the direction of the force on a current-carrying rod to the direction of the current and of the magnetic field.

spec.question: A positively-charged particle (alpha-particle) projected towards west is deflected towards north by a magnetic field. What is the direction of the magnetic field?
options: Towards south
Towards east
Downward
Upward
spec.answer: Upward
spec.explanation: Use Fleming's left-hand rule. The current is towards west and the force is towards north; the magnetic field must be upward.
spec.expected_understanding: Apply Fleming's left-hand rule to a positively charged particle.

spec.question: When is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
options: When the current is parallel to the magnetic field.
When the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
When the current is zero.
When the conductor is outside the field.
spec.answer: When the current is at right angles to the magnetic field.
spec.explanation: The displacement of the rod is largest when the direction of current is at right angles to the direction of the magnetic field.
spec.expected_understanding: State the condition for the largest magnetic force on a conductor.

spec.question: An electron beam moves horizontally from the back wall towards the front wall of a chamber. It is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of the magnetic field?
options: Upward
Downward
Towards the front wall
Towards the back wall
spec.answer: Downward
spec.explanation: The electron current is opposite to the electron motion. Using Fleming's left-hand rule with the force to the right gives a downward magnetic field.
spec.expected_understanding: Use the left-hand rule with the current opposite to electron motion.

spec.question: Which rule gives the direction of the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor, and which rule gives the direction of force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field?
options: Fleming's left-hand rule; right-hand thumb rule
Right-hand thumb rule; Fleming's left-hand rule
Right-hand thumb rule; right-hand thumb rule
Fleming's left-hand rule; Fleming's left-hand rule
spec.answer: Right-hand thumb rule; Fleming's left-hand rule
spec.explanation: The right-hand thumb rule gives the field around a straight conductor, and Fleming's left-hand rule gives the force on a current-carrying conductor. The chapter does not state a rule for current induced by rotation; it only names electric generator as a device.
spec.expected_understanding: Match each rule to its use.

paragraphs: In homes, electric power comes through mains, either by overhead poles or underground cables. The live wire usually has red insulation and is positive. The neutral wire has black insulation and is negative. In our country the potential difference between them is 220 V. The supply is AC at 220 V with a frequency of 50 Hz.

At the meter-board, the wires pass through an electricity meter and a main fuse. Through the main switch they connect to line wires. Often two circuits are used: a 15 A circuit for high-power appliances such as geysers and air coolers, and a 5 A circuit for bulbs and fans.

The earth wire has green insulation and is connected to a metal plate deep in the earth. It is a safety measure for appliances with metallic bodies. It provides a low-resistance path so that any leakage of current to the metallic body does not give the user a severe shock.

Appliances are connected in parallel across live and neutral so that each gets the same potential difference. Each appliance has its own switch. A fuse prevents damage due to overloading. The Joule heating in the fuse melts it and breaks the circuit.

Short-circuiting occurs when the live and neutral wires touch directly; the current increases abruptly. Overloading can also occur from an accidental hike in supply voltage or by connecting too many appliances to one socket.

spec.question: Name two safety measures commonly used in electric circuits and appliances.
options: Fuse and earth wire
Live wire and neutral wire
Red insulation and black insulation
5 A and 15 A
spec.answer: Fuse and earth wire
spec.explanation: A fuse protects against overloading by melting, and the earth wire provides a safety path for leakage current.
spec.expected_understanding: Recall two domestic safety measures.

spec.question: How does an electric fuse protect a domestic circuit?
options: The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it and breaks the electric circuit.
The fuse stores the extra current and supplies it later.
The fuse raises the supply voltage.
The fuse connects the live wire to the earth wire.
spec.answer: The Joule heating that takes place in the fuse melts it and breaks the electric circuit.
spec.explanation: A fuse prevents damage to the appliances and the circuit due to overloading by stopping the flow of unduly high electric current; the Joule heating in the fuse melts it to break the circuit.
spec.expected_understanding: Explain the working of an electric fuse as a safety device against overloading.

spec.question: What precaution should be taken to avoid the overloading of domestic electric circuits?
options: Connect too many appliances to a single socket.
Avoid connecting too many appliances to a single socket and use a fuse of proper rating.
Replace the earth wire with a live wire.
Use only 15 A circuits for bulbs.
spec.answer: Avoid connecting too many appliances to a single socket and use a fuse of proper rating.
spec.explanation: Overloading can be caused by connecting too many appliances to a single socket; a fuse protects the circuit if current becomes too high.
spec.expected_understanding: State a precaution against overloading.

spec.question: At the time of short circuit, the current in the circuit
options: reduces substantially.
does not change.
increases heavily.
vary continuously.
spec.answer: increases heavily.
spec.explanation: When live and neutral wires touch directly, the current in the circuit abruptly increases.
spec.expected_understanding: Know the current change at a short circuit.

spec.question: When does an electric short circuit occur?
options: When the live wire and neutral wire come into direct contact.
When the fuse melts.
When the earth wire is connected to a metal plate.
When the main switch is off.
spec.answer: When the live wire and neutral wire come into direct contact.
spec.explanation: Direct contact between live and neutral wires is short-circuiting; this can happen when insulation is damaged or an appliance has a fault.
spec.expected_understanding: Define short circuit.

spec.question: What is the function of an earth wire, and why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
options: It carries the normal current and increases the supply voltage.
It provides a low-resistance path for leakage current so the user may not get a severe shock.
It melts when current is too high.
It makes the appliance live.
spec.answer: It provides a low-resistance path for leakage current so the user may not get a severe shock.
spec.explanation: The metallic body is connected to the earth wire. If current leaks to the body, the earth wire keeps its potential at that of the earth and protects the user.
spec.expected_understanding: Explain the purpose of the earth wire.

spec.question: Which statement is true?
options: The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines.
A wire with green insulation is usually the live wire of an electric supply.
Both statements are true.
Neither statement is true.
spec.answer: The field at the centre of a long circular coil carrying current will be parallel straight lines.
spec.explanation: At the centre of a current-carrying circular coil the field lines appear as parallel straight lines. The green-insulated wire is the earth wire, not the live wire.
spec.expected_understanding: Check true-false statements about coil fields and wire colours.

paragraphs: Electric currents in the body, even weak ion currents along nerve cells, produce magnetic fields. These fields are very weak, about one-billionth of the earth's magnetic field. The heart and the brain are two main organs where the magnetic field produced is significant.
The magnetic field inside the body is used in Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to obtain images of different body parts. Analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.

spec.question: Which technique uses the magnetic field inside the body to obtain images of different body parts for medical diagnosis?
options: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
Electric fuse
Solenoid
Oersted unit
spec.answer: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
spec.explanation: MRI uses the magnetic field inside the body to obtain images; analysis of these images helps in medical diagnosis.
spec.expected_understanding: Recall the medical use of magnetic fields described in the chapter.
